h1: Reviews and ratings: managing them for a brewery
title: Managing Brewery Reviews and Ratings | Craft Beer School
desc: How a brewery can earn good reviews honestly, ask for them without rewards, reply to praise and complaints and learn from what customers write.
teaser: Reviews are public, permanent and read before people visit. A calm, honest routine will serve you better than any trick.
standfirst: Most new visitors read your reviews before they read anything else. You cannot control what people write, but you can earn better reviews and reply well to all of them.
sections:
A rating and a few recent comments often decide whether someone walks in. Reviews also feed local search results, as part of what makes a profile look relevant and trusted. We cannot promise any effect on ranking, but a taproom with recent honest reviews looks alive.

Reviews are also free research. They tell you what visitors like and what frustrates them, in their words.

Good reviews follow good visits. The beer cold and fresh, a clean glass, staff who know the list, a table that is ready when promised. Fix the basics first. A brewery that serves a stale, warm beer will not be saved by asking for reviews.

Brewing quality matters here. Beer that has picked up oxidation or a buttery note will draw a comment that sticks. Our guide to beer off flavours shows what customers may be tasting.

It is fine to ask happy customers to leave a review. Put a small card or a QR code at the table or on the receipt that links to your profile. Ask staff to mention it naturally to people who say they enjoyed their visit.

Do not offer free drinks, discounts or prizes in exchange for reviews. Most platforms forbid it. It can lead to reviews being removed. Do not ask only happy customers while steering unhappy ones elsewhere, which many platforms prohibit. Never write reviews yourself or ask staff and friends to do so. Fake reviews breach platform rules and can break consumer protection law in many places.

Reply to positive reviews briefly and by name where you can. Mention something specific so that it does not read as a template.

For negative reviews, take a breath, wait until you are calm and reply in public with three parts: thanks, a short acknowledgement of the problem and an offer to talk offline with a contact. Do not argue, blame, reveal personal details or accuse the reviewer of lying. Future readers judge you by the reply as much as by the complaint.

If a review breaks the platform's rules, such as spam, abuse or a review of a visit that never happened, report it through the platform. Removal is not guaranteed. Meanwhile reply politely and factually. Keep a record of what you reported and when.

Once a month, read the new reviews and tally the themes: freshness, price, service, noise, waiting time, food. A theme that appears three times is a pattern, not a one-off. Share it with staff and pick one thing to change. Compare with what you see in competitor analysis, since your rivals' reviews show where you can do better.

Record changes and watch whether the theme fades. That is a good test of whether your fix worked.

Give one person the job of checking reviews each week, with a backup. Agree a short guide for replies: tone, what to offer and who to escalate to. Share good reviews with staff by name, because recognition keeps standards up. For complaints about safety, harassment or an incident, tell the owner at once and follow your licence conditions.

Keep a simple log: date, platform, rating, theme, reply sent. Over a few months it shows whether your changes make a difference and gives you real evidence for decisions about hours, staffing and the beer list.

Do not respond in anger. Do not post replies that reveal a customer's identity or the details of their visit. Do not ask friends to swing your rating. Do not delete negative comments on your own channels and leave the praise. A brewery with a few honest complaints and polite replies looks more believable than one with a perfect score.

Never celebrate heavy drinking in replies. If a review mentions someone who had too much or an incident, respond with care. Follow your licence conditions. Keep your replies the same in tone as your brand. For wider work on keeping visitors coming, read SEO mistakes drinks websites make.
faqs: Can I delete a bad review?
Not yourself. You can reply. You can report reviews that break the platform's rules.
Is it allowed to give a discount for a review?
Most platforms forbid rewards for reviews. Check the current policy of each platform and avoid it.
Within a day or two is a good aim. Speed matters less than a calm, honest reply.
